    Chapter 2

    A Quick Trip Through History

    🤔 A cipher with 400 septillion possible keys was cracked in the 9th century, with pen and paper. How?

    • ⏱️ ~6 min
    • 📚 7 sections
    • 🎮 5 interactive
    • ⭐ 240 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    Old ciphers are easy to understand and easy to break. Each one teaches a lesson that still matters today.

    2.1The Caesar cipher (about 50 BC)#

    Julius Caesar reportedly protected military messages by shifting every letter three places down the alphabet:

    So:

    The algorithm is "shift letters." The key is "3."

    How to break it: there are only 25 possible shifts. An attacker just tries them all. This is a brute-force attack: trying every possible key.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): encrypt, decrypt and brute-force a Caesar cipher.

    Python
    def caesar(text, shift):
    out = ""
    for ch in text.upper():
        if ch.isalpha():
            out += chr((ord(ch) - ord('A') + shift) % 26 + ord('A'))
        else:
            out += ch
    return out

secret = caesar("ATTACK AT DAWN", 3)
print(secret)                 # DWWDFN DW GDZQ
print(caesar(secret, -3))     # ATTACK AT DAWN

# Brute force: try every key
for shift in range(1, 26):
    print(shift, caesar(secret, -shift))
# ...
# 3 ATTACK AT DAWN   <- the only line that makes sense

    💡 Lesson 1: If the number of possible keys is small, the cipher is broken, no matter how clever it looks.

    2.2Substitution ciphers and frequency analysis (9th century)#

    Instead of shifting, scramble the whole alphabet randomly:

    Now there are 26! (26 × 25 × 24 × … × 1) possible keys, about 403 septillion (4 × 10²⁶). Trying them all is hopeless by hand.

    It was still broken, by the Arab scholar Al-Kindi around 850 AD. His insight: in any language, some letters appear more often than others. In English, E is the most common letter (about 12.7% of letters), followed by T, A, O, I, N.

    If the most common symbol in a long ciphertext is T, it probably stands for E. Work through the frequent letters, guess short words like "THE" and "AND," and the whole message unravels.

    💡 Lesson 2: A huge key space isn't enough. If the ciphertext leaks patterns from the plaintext, attackers will exploit them. Modern ciphers must make ciphertext look completely random.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…

    2.3The Vigenère cipher (1500s): "the indecipherable cipher"#

    Use a keyword to apply a different Caesar shift to each letter. With the keyword LEMON (L=11, E=4, M=12, O=14, N=13):

    The two Ts in "ATTACK" become different letters (X and F), which defeats simple frequency analysis. It was called "le chiffre indéchiffrable" for 300 years.

    It was broken in the 1800s (by Charles Babbage and Friedrich Kasiski). Because the keyword repeats, patterns reappear at regular intervals. Find the keyword length, split the text into groups, and each group is just a Caesar cipher.

    💡 Lesson 3: Repetition is the enemy. Any time a key or pattern repeats, an attacker gets a foothold. You'll see this again with "nonce reuse" in Chapters 4 and 5.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    2.4The Enigma machine (World War II)#

    The German military used Enigma, an electro-mechanical machine with rotating wheels (rotors). Each key press moved the rotors, so the substitution changed with every single letter. A typical configuration had about 159 quintillion (1.59 × 10²⁰) possible settings.

    It was broken anyway: first by Polish mathematicians (Marian Rejewski and colleagues, in the 1930s), then at Bletchley Park in Britain by Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman and thousands of others. They used early computing machines ("bombes") plus three weaknesses:

    1. A design flaw: Enigma never encrypted a letter as itself. That small pattern ruled out huge numbers of possibilities.
    2. Predictable messages ("cribs"): many messages contained standard phrases such as weather reports, so analysts could guess parts of the plaintext.
    3. Human mistakes: operators reused settings or picked lazy ones.

    💡 Lesson 4: Systems usually fail through design shortcuts and human habits, not because someone tried every key. This is still true. Chapter 18 is full of modern examples.

    2.5The one-time pad: perfect secrecy (with a catch)#

    There is exactly one cipher that is mathematically proven unbreakable: the one-time pad.

    The rules:

    1. The key is truly random.
    2. The key is as long as the message.
    3. The key is used once and then destroyed.

    You combine each letter (or bit) of the message with the matching letter (or bit) of the key. Without the key, every possible plaintext of that length is equally likely. The ciphertext XMCKL could be "HELLO," "PIZZA" or "TANKS." There is no way to tell, even with infinite computing power. Claude Shannon proved this in 1949.

    The catch: you need a secret key as long as everything you'll ever send, and you must deliver it securely in advance. If you can do that, you could almost deliver the message itself that way. That's why one-time pads are used only in rare cases, such as the Cold War Moscow–Washington hotline.

    📜 True story: Venona. During the 1940s, the Soviet Union, under wartime pressure, printed some one-time pad pages twice. US analysts noticed, and over decades decrypted thousands of Soviet messages, exposing spies including those in the atomic bomb project. Reusing a "one-time" pad destroyed its perfect security.

    💡 Lesson 5: "One-time" really means one time. Reusing a key that was meant to be used once is one of the most common ways cryptography fails.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Classical ciphers: the scorecard

    ❌ Avoid
    Caesar cipher

    Shift every letter by k

    • Dead simple; great for teaching
    • Encrypt and decrypt by hand
    • Only 25 keys: brute-forced in seconds
    • Keeps letter frequencies intact
    Best for: Puzzles and kids’ secret notes
    ❌ Avoid
    Substitution

    Scramble the whole alphabet

    • 26! ≈ 4 × 10²⁶ keys
    • Defeats brute force by hand
    • Frequency analysis breaks it (Al-Kindi, ~850 AD)
    • Same letter → same symbol every time
    Best for: Newspaper cryptograms
    ❌ Avoid
    Vigenère

    A different shift per letter

    • Flattens simple letter frequencies
    • Resisted attack for ~300 years
    • The keyword repeats → Kasiski / Babbage attack
    • Short keywords fall quickly
    Best for: History lessons
    ❌ Avoid
    Enigma

    Rotors change the substitution each key press

    • ~1.59 × 10²⁰ settings
    • Different substitution for every letter
    • Never encrypted a letter as itself
    • Predictable cribs and lazy operators
    Best for: Museums and movies
    💡 Concept
    One-time pad

    Truly random key as long as the message, used once

    • Mathematically proven unbreakable (Shannon, 1949)
    • Secure even against infinite computing power
    • Key must be as long as all your messages
    • Must be delivered securely in advance
    • Reuse destroys it (Venona)
    Best for: Rare diplomatic hotlines

    2.6The computer age#

    Modern cryptography began when computers made it possible to do enormous amounts of scrambling very fast. A few milestones:

    1. 1949
      Claude Shannon publishes the mathematical theory of secrecy

      Why it matters: Crypto becomes a science

    2. 1973
      Clifford Cocks at British intelligence (GCHQ) secretly invents what we now call RSA

      Why it matters: Kept classified until 1997

    3. 1976
      Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman publish "New Directions in Cryptography"

      Why it matters: Public-key cryptography and key exchange are born (Chapter 10)

    4. 1977
      DES becomes the US standard cipher; RSA is published by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman

      Why it matters: Strong crypto becomes available to businesses

    5. 1985
      Elliptic-curve cryptography proposed (Koblitz, Miller)

      Why it matters: Smaller, faster public keys

    6. 1991
      Phil Zimmermann releases PGP

      Why it matters: Strong email encryption for everyone

    7. 1995
      Netscape releases SSL

      Why it matters: The ancestor of HTTPS

    8. 1998
      The EFF builds "Deep Crack" and breaks DES in 56 hours

      Why it matters: 56-bit keys are officially too short

    9. 2001
      AES becomes the new standard

      Why it matters: Still the world's most-used cipher

    10. 2008
      The Bitcoin paper is published

      Why it matters: Cryptography as the basis for money

    11. 2013
      Snowden revelations about mass surveillance

      Why it matters: Big push to encrypt everything

    12. 2015
      Let's Encrypt launches free, automated certificates

      Why it matters: HTTPS becomes the default for the web

    13. 2018
      TLS 1.3 is published

      Why it matters: Faster, simpler, safer HTTPS

    14. 2024
      NIST publishes the first post-quantum standards

      Why it matters: Preparing for quantum computers (Chapter 17)

    ✔ section read

    2.7Lessons from history, in one list#

    1. Small key spaces get brute-forced. (Caesar)
    2. Patterns leak. Ciphertext must look perfectly random. (Substitution)
    3. Repetition is dangerous. (Vigenère, Venona)
    4. Humans and shortcuts are the weakest link. (Enigma)
    5. Secret designs don't stay secret. Rely only on the secrecy of the key. (Kerckhoffs)
